lede: A girl who dug clay out of the fields near her village and modelled it into heads, became one of the boldest sculptors of her age, and spent her last thirty years locked in an asylum while her family kept her there.

ps: Camille Claudel was born on 8 December 1864 in Fère-en-Tardenois, in the Aisne in northern France. Her younger brother was the poet and diplomat Paul Claudel.

She came to Paris to study sculpture in 1881 and around 1883 joined the workshop of Auguste Rodin. She was his student, assistant, model and lover for about ten years, and made her own works of startling movement and feeling, such as The Waltz and The Age of Maturity.

After their break she worked alone in growing poverty and isolation, and destroyed much of her own work. In March 1913, a week after her father died, her family had her committed. She spent thirty years in asylums and died at Montdevergues, near Avignon, on 19 October 1943, aged 78.

Her father, Louis-Prosper Claudel, was a civil servant who moved the family from town to town. He believed in her talent. Her mother, Louise-Athénaïse, never accepted that her daughter wanted to be an artist.
As a child in Villeneuve-sur-Fère she made figures from local clay and made her brother and sister pose. Paul later wrote of her forceful, commanding temper.

In Nogent-sur-Seine, where the family lived in the late 1870s, the sculptor Alfred Boucher saw her work and encouraged her. In 1881 her mother moved to Paris with the children so that Camille could study and Paul could go to a good school.

Paris, 1881. She studied at the Académie Colarossi, one of the few private schools that took women, and shared a studio with other young women sculptors, several of them English, including Jessie Lipscomb.
1882. When Boucher left for Italy he asked Rodin to take over teaching the young women. Rodin was 42; Camille was 17 or 18.

Rodin's workshop, around 1883. She joined his studio, working on hands and feet for The Gates of Hell and The Burghers of Calais. They became lovers. Rodin would not leave his long-time companion Rose Beuret.

ps.t: Around 1892. The love affair ended. She may have had a pregnancy that did not go to term, perhaps an abortion.
ps.why: It rests on hints in family letters and later writings; there is no clear record.

ps: 1893. She showed The Waltz and Clotho at the Salon. Critics began to speak of her as a sculptor in her own right.
By 1898 she and Rodin had parted for good. She came to believe that he was stealing her ideas and plotting against her.

From about 1905. In her flat on the Quai de Bourbon in Paris, her home since 1899, she lived alone with cats, little money and fewer visitors. Each summer she smashed many of the works she had made that year.

March 1913. Her father died on 2 March; the family did not tell her. On 10 March, with a doctor's certificate and the request of her mother and brother, two attendants took her from her flat to the asylum of Ville-Évrard near Paris. In 1914, because of the war, she was moved to Montdevergues near Avignon.

1913 to 1943. Doctors more than once suggested she could go home to her family. Her mother refused. Camille wrote letters begging to be freed. Her mother never visited; Paul came rarely. She died in 1943, during the wartime hunger that killed many patients in French asylums.
Bust of Rodin (1888 to 1889), a rugged, powerful head. Rodin himself admired it.
Sakuntala (1888), a kneeling man embracing a woman who leans into him, from an Indian drama. It won an honourable mention at the Salon. A marble version is called Vertumnus and Pomona.
The Waltz (1889 to 1905), a couple dancing so close and so tilted that they seem about to fall. She made several versions.
The Age of Maturity (1893 to about 1903). An old man is pulled away by a winged old woman while a young kneeling woman reaches after him. Many people, including Paul, read it as her break with Rodin.
The Gossips (1893 to 1905), four tiny women huddled in a corner, telling secrets, and The Wave (1897 to 1903), three bathers under a breaking wave of green onyx.
Clotho (1893), one of the three Fates, an ancient, bony woman tangled in the threads of life.
Auguste Rodin (1840 to 1917), her teacher, collaborator and lover. Influence passed both ways in their work. After they parted he quietly helped her get commissions and buyers.

Paul Claudel (1868 to 1955), her brother, a Catholic poet and diplomat. He loved her and admired her art, but agreed to her commitment and kept her there. In 1951 he helped arrange an exhibition of her work at the Musée Rodin.
Louise-Athénaïse Claudel, her mother, who opposed her career and refused her release.
Louis-Prosper Claudel (1826 to 1913), her father, who supported her and sent her money until he died.
Jessie Lipscomb (1861 to 1952), English sculptor, studio friend and travel companion.
Women could not enter the official École des Beaux-Arts until 1897, and drawing from nude models was thought improper for them. A woman sculptor needed money for studios, clay, marble and casting.
In late nineteenth century France, families and doctors could commit a person to an asylum on a doctor's certificate at the family's request, under an 1838 law.
During the Second World War, many thousands of patients in French psychiatric hospitals died of hunger and cold, as food went to the army and the occupiers.
For decades she was remembered mainly as Rodin's mistress. Biographies, exhibitions and the 1988 film Camille Claudel with Isabelle Adjani brought her work back into view.
The Musée Camille Claudel opened in 2017 in Nogent-sur-Seine, in the town where she began. The Musée Rodin in Paris also has a room of her sculpture.
Her remains were placed in a shared grave at Montfavet and were never recovered.

myths.t: The break hurt her deeply and she came to fear him, but no single cause explains her illness. Poverty, isolation and her family all played a part, and it was her family, not Rodin, who had her committed and kept her there.
She trained before she met him and made major works of her own design, which critics of the 1890s praised on their own merits.

myths.c: Doctors kept her locked up because she was dangerous.
myths.t: She was diagnosed with delusions of persecution, and modern writers cannot know what illness she had. But her doctors suggested release more than once, and her mother said no.
She believed he did. Some hands and feet in his work may be hers, from studio work, but no case of him signing her sculpture is proven.
